section.title: Properties of the integral
section.p: The integral was born from sums. Its basic properties are inherited from sums.
A Riemann sum has the form
Finite sums are linear. They can be split into pieces. They preserve inequalities. They respect symmetry. When the Riemann sums approach a limit, those same habits survive in the integral.
This section is not a list of tricks. It is the arithmetic of accumulation.

exercise.title: Why can accumulation be split, and why does reversing limits change the sign?

statement.p: Accumulation from a to b is accumulation from a to c plus accumulation from c to b. Reversing the limits multiplies by -1. In your own words, why do these rules treat the interval as oriented, and why is there no accumulation from a point to itself?

hint.p: Moving from a to b is the opposite of moving from b to a. With no width, there is no accumulation.

exercise.title: Why does an odd function integrate to zero on a symmetric interval?

statement.p: Even functions double on [-a,a]; odd functions cancel. In your own words, why is that a statement about signed area and symmetry rather than a computational shortcut that happens to work, and why must the interval itself be symmetric for the rule to apply?

hint.p: An odd graph is symmetric through the origin, so the signed area on the left cancels the signed area on the right. An even graph has matching contributions on both sides.

subsection.title: Where the properties come from
subsection.p: The properties of the integral are not mysterious. They are the properties of finite sums surviving a limiting process.

md.mrow: \hline \sum (Af_j+Bg_j)\Delta x_j = A\sum f_j\Delta x_j+B\sum g_j\Delta x_j \amp \int_a^b (Af+Bg)\,dx = A\int_a^b f\,dx+B\int_a^b g\,dx
[2mm] \text{a long sum can be split into shorter sums} \amp \int_a^b f\,dx = \int_a^c f\,dx+\int_c^b f\,dx
[2mm] f_j\le g_j \text{ for all }j \Rightarrow \sum f_j\Delta x_j\le \sum g_j\Delta x_j \amp f\le g \Rightarrow \int_a^b f\,dx\le \int_a^b g\,dx

subsection.p: These rules make the integral usable before we know many exact antiderivatives. They allow us to split, estimate, compare, and simplify accumulated quantities.
One question remains before we can rely on the integral fully:
Continuous functions do. So do many functions with jumps. But not every bounded function is integrable. The next section explains where the line is.
